children: South Korean policymakers are ratcheting up verbal interventions to stabilise domestic financial markets amid an accelerating global bond selloff, vowing to curb short-term Treasury bond issuance and deploy market support measures if needed.
Finance minister Lee Hyoung-il on Friday said the government was ready to "consider a further reduction in (Treasury bond) issuance volume if necessary".
The comment comes after the ministry slashed October's Treasury bond issuance by 5 trillion won ($3.67 billion) in a statement on Thursday.

Lee emphasised that the government, in close coordination with the Bank of Korea, was ready to deploy emergency market stabilisation tools — including large-scale buy backs or early debt redemptions if the rout deepened.

South Korea's benchmark three-year bond yield surged by 11 basis points to 4.11% on Monday after the domestic bond market reopened following the national Chuseok holidays, the highest level since November 2022, joining a global selloff as elevated oil prices stoked concern over inflation.
During South Korea's holiday market closure, resilient US economic growth and sticky inflation components prompted market participants to price in a more aggressive Federal Reserve policy path.
Seoul officials intensified verbal interventions throughout this week to cap market volatility.
On Friday, Lee warned that prolonged high interest rates and widening credit spreads could severely impair refinancing conditions for households with weak credit profiles.
The three-year yield stood at 4.01% on Friday morning, hovering near a four-year high reached on Monday.
